title: SEBI Finalises Digital KYC From Abroad for NRIs, Effective December 3
excerpt: A final SEBI circular dated November 4 replaces the August proposal: eligible NRIs, OCIs and foreign nationals in FATF-compliant countries can onboard digitally from overseas, with portable KYC records.
body:
• SEBI's final circular dated November 4, 2026 lets NRIs, OCIs and foreign nationals in FATF-compliant countries complete investment KYC digitally from abroad, without being physically in India.
  • The rules take effect on December 3, 2026 — this is the final decision, not the August consultation proposal, which only invited comments until September 4.
  • KYC records become portable: an investor can reuse a record held via a KYC Registration Agency or the Central KYC Records Registry with another intermediary, even if not every attribute is yet tagged validated.
  • You will still need PAN verification, a passport copy (plus OCI card where applicable) and video verification with an authorised official; residents of FATF non-compliant countries stay on the old process.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has issued its final circular easing Know Your Client (KYC) rules for overseas investors, allowing eligible Non-Resident Indians (NRIs), Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) and foreign nationals to complete digital onboarding from abroad without being physically present in India. The circular, dated November 4, 2026, takes effect on December 3, 2026.

This is a different step from the proposal covered earlier this year. In August, SEBI published a consultation paper inviting public comments until September 4, and no final circular had been issued at that point. The November 4 circular now settles the framework, sets the start date, and supersedes the earlier December 10, 2025 relaxation that covered only re-KYC geo-tagging for NRIs. The full circular text is reproduced by TaxGuru, with a summary from FinBrooks.

Who is affected, exactly

The change covers individual Persons Resident Outside India (PROIs) — NRIs, OCIs and foreign nationals — who are located in a country compliant with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards and who are onboarding with a SEBI-registered intermediary, such as for a demat, trading or mutual fund relationship. The same process also applies to re-KYC for existing clients in FATF-compliant countries. Clients residing in FATF non-compliant countries are expressly excluded: the existing KYC process continues for them. Individual foreign nationals who seek registration as Foreign Portfolio Investors remain under SEBI's separate FPI framework.

What changed, precisely

Until now, SEBI's KYC Master Circular required an intermediary to ensure that during digital KYC the client's physical location was in India, which in practice blocked complete digital onboarding from overseas. From December 3, an intermediary may accept digital submission of KYC information and supporting documents from an eligible PROI client abroad.

Three other changes matter. First, portability: a KYC Registration Agency (KRA) will tag each attribute — such as PAN, passport or address — as validated when it has been verified against an official or source database, but all KYC records are portable and can be shared with another intermediary irrespective of whether every attribute is validated. Second, reliance: an intermediary may rely on KYC done by another SEBI-registered intermediary, using a record obtained from a KRA, or on KYC done by an entity regulated by another financial-sector regulator, using a record from the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCRR). Third, verification moves to video: where physical in-person verification is not feasible, Video In Person Verification (VIPV) may be used, with the client's consent recorded, live geo-tagging, checks against spoofed IP addresses, VPNs and proxies, face-liveness checks, end-to-end encryption, an authorised official present throughout, and concurrent audit.

What you will still need to provide

Digital does not mean document-free. The intermediary must collect and verify your PAN against the Income Tax database, collect a copy of your passport and, where applicable, your OCI card, and treat your overseas address as your current address for proof of address. The KYC form can be submitted physically, as a scanned copy under electronic signature, or as a digital form under electronic signature. A specimen signature submitted digitally must be signed wet before the intermediary during VIPV so it can be matched. Documents not in English must be translated into English and attested before submission. The intermediary remains ultimately responsible for your KYC, including enhanced due diligence based on your risk profile, and must pass the completed KYC information to the KRA within three working days.

What to do next

If you are an NRI, OCI or foreign national in an FATF-compliant country, do not start a new onboarding expecting the remote route before December 3, 2026 — KYC completed before the circular takes effect stays under the existing provisions. From December 3, ask your chosen intermediary whether its app or website supports PROI digital onboarding and VIPV, and have your PAN, passport and, if relevant, OCI card ready. If you already hold a KYC record with another intermediary, ask whether it can be fetched from the KRA or CKYCRR instead of repeating the full process. SEBI says the circular is available on its website, sebi.gov.in, under Legal and Circulars.
